sections.title: Family membership enquiry
sections.context: A telephone-style conversation at a sports centre. A customer asks a receptionist about a family membership and the receptionist completes the enquiry form.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Good afternoon, Riverside Sports Centre. How can I help you?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Hello. I'd like some information about family membership, please. My wife and I have two children, and we'd like to swim together at weekends.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Of course. I'll take a few details so I can fill in the enquiry form. First, can I have your family name?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It's Okafor. O-K-A-F-O-R.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Thank you. And what's the best contact number for you?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It's zero seven seven zero zero nine zero zero one five two. That's my mobile, so it's the best one to ring during the day.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Got it. And how many children will be joining?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Two. Our daughter is nine and our son is six. Both of them can swim a little, but they're not very confident yet.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: That's no problem. We have lessons for every level. The family package covers two adults and up to three children under sixteen, so you're well within that. Which day would suit you for swimming?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Saturday would be best, because the children don't have school. Is there a quieter time in the day?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: The pool is quietest early in the morning. Most families arrive just before the first lesson. What time would you normally arrive?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: We'd aim for half past seven, so we can be in the water by eight.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Half past seven is a good time for a quiet session. The monthly fee for the family package is eighty-four pounds. That includes unlimited swimming and gym access for both adults.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That's reasonable. Does it include lessons for the children?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Lessons are an extra, so the fee only covers access. But I can add the children's course at a reduced rate if you'd like it.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Let's leave that for now. When could we start?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Membership can start on the first of September. If you join before then, the first week is free.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The first of September is perfect. Can we also choose a locker?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Yes, lockers are assigned by number. Which one would you like?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Locker twenty-two, if it's free. It's near the family changing room, which is handy with two children.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Let me check. Yes, twenty-two is available. Now, how would you like to pay?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I'd prefer to pay by direct debit, so the money comes out automatically each month.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: No problem. One last question: is there any medical condition we should know about for anyone in the family?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, our son has asthma. He carries an inhaler, and I'd like the lifeguards to know about it.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Thank you, I'll note that on the record, and the lifeguards will be informed. Is there anything else I can help you with?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No, that's everything. Thanks very much.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: You're welcome. We'll send you a confirmation by email this evening.

sections.title: Orientation talk at a botanical garden
sections.context: A volunteer guide gives a short orientation talk to visitors before a guided tour of a botanical garden, explaining the history, the layout and practical arrangements.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Greenwood Botanical Gardens. My name is Helen, and I'll be your guide for this morning's tour. Before we set off, I'd like to give you a little background and a few practical points, because some of you are new to the gardens and the layout can be a bit confusing at first.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The gardens were originally built in 1880 as a private estate for the Harrington family. They loved plants, and over the years they collected species from all over the world. When the last family member died, the estate was given to the city, and it opened to the public in 1923.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: So, as you can see, the gardens still have a very grand, old-fashioned feel in places, especially around the lake.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The tour takes about an hour and a half and covers the four main areas. We'll start at the visitor centre, not at the main gate, so please make sure you've found us before you wander off. The tour begins at ten o'clock sharp, because the glasshouse opens for a short time at the beginning of the morning, and I want to be inside while it's quiet.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Speaking of the glasshouse, which is in the north-west corner of the gardens and a bit of a walk from here, I need to ask you something. It's full of delicate plants, and large bags can knock the leaves and damage the displays.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Could you please leave any large bags in the lockers at the visitor centre? Small handbags and cameras are fine to bring with you. The lockers are free, but they take one pound coins, so please check you have some change.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Now, the most popular part of the tour, especially with children, is the butterfly enclosure. It's a warm, netted area, and there are around forty species flying around at this time of year. Please don't touch the butterflies, and keep the gate closed behind you.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: If you're interested in photography, this is the best spot on the whole tour.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: After the butterflies, we'll walk down to the lily pond by the lake. The lake is quite deep in the middle, so please keep children close to the path. The pond is home to several species of water lily, and some of them only flower at night, which is a lovely thing to see if you come back in the evening.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: You'll find the sensory garden on the way back. It's designed for visitors who are blind or partially sighted, but everyone is welcome to use it. The plants have strong scents and different textures, and there are labels in large print and in braille.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: It sits just behind the glasshouse, so we'll pass it on our way to the herb garden.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Finally, the tea room is on the far side of the central lawn, directly opposite the visitor centre. It's a great place to rest your feet at the end of the tour. Most of the cakes are made with herbs from our own herb garden, which is a nice touch.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Please note that the tea room closes at four, while the gardens themselves stay open until six.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Let me finish with a few reminders. The guidebook costs four pounds, but you can borrow a free map at the desk if you don't want to buy anything. We'll finish the tour at the gift shop, which is next to the main gate.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: After that you're free to explore on your own. Please meet back at the visitor centre if you want to join the afternoon tour, which starts at quarter past one.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: So, to recap: be at the visitor centre for ten o'clock, leave your large bags in the lockers, and keep your eyes open for the water lilies. Does anyone have any questions before we set off?

sections.title: Tutorial on a library redesign project
sections.context: Two students meet their tutor to discuss the planning of a group project on redesigning a local library, including the survey, the presentation and the site visit.

transcript.speaker: Sophie
transcript.text: Hi Dr Walsh, thanks for seeing us. We've started the library project, and we'd like to check our approach before we go any further.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Of course. Let's see where you are. Tell me about the survey first.

transcript.speaker: Sophie
transcript.text: We've done one, but I'm not confident in it. We asked only fifty people, and most of them were students who use the building every day.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: That's the main problem. Fifty is too small to tell you much, and if the sample is mostly students, the results won't reflect the wider community. You need to reach families, older residents and people who don't use the library at all.

transcript.speaker: Sophie
transcript.text: Right, we'll redo it. Tom wants to include a short video of the building in the presentation, to show its current state.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: A video can help people picture the place, but it doesn't tell the audience anything new. Something more interactive would work better.

transcript.speaker: Sophie
transcript.text: That's what I thought too. I'd like to run a live survey during the presentation, so the audience can vote on the options in real time.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: I like that. It makes the presentation engaging, and it gives you immediate feedback. What else are you planning?

transcript.speaker: Sophie
transcript.text: We want to compare the costs of the three options.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Yes, definitely. A cost comparison is essential, because the council will want to see value for money. Don't bother with a model of the building, though. It takes ages to make, and your audience won't need it.

transcript.speaker: Sophie
transcript.text: Agreed. We won't do a model, and the map of the bus routes isn't relevant either, so we'll leave it out.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Good. Now, the opening hours. You mentioned that the library closes at six. Have you looked at how it's used in the evenings?

transcript.speaker: Sophie
transcript.text: Not yet. Our assumption is that evenings are quiet, but we haven't checked.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Then look at the evening use figures before you decide anything. If evening use is high, the case for extending the hours becomes much stronger. Don't rely only on what you think.

transcript.speaker: Sophie
transcript.text: OK, we'll do that. We've also walked around the site and made some notes. Shall I go through the problems?

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Please. Let's start with the entrance.

transcript.speaker: Sophie
transcript.text: The ground floor is the first problem. There's a side entrance, but there's no step-free access there, so wheelchair users have to go round the back.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: That's a serious issue, and it should be highlighted. What about upstairs?

transcript.speaker: Sophie
transcript.text: The upper floor has plenty of space, but the lighting is too dim for reading. Several people told us they avoid it for that reason.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Lighting is often cheap to fix, so that could be a quick win. What about the outside?

transcript.speaker: Sophie
transcript.text: The reading garden is pleasant, but it floods after heavy rain, so it can't be used for much of the winter.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: That will be expensive to fix, so present it as a separate option. And the basement?

transcript.speaker: Sophie
transcript.text: The basement is the children's area. It's mainly used by parents with pushchairs, and the staff think it should be bigger.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Good. Now, the report. When is the deadline?

transcript.speaker: Sophie
transcript.text: It's due on Friday, and we have to submit it online by then.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Remember the word limit. The report must be no more than two thousand words, and the appendices don't count towards it.

transcript.speaker: Sophie
transcript.text: Got it. Thanks, that's really helpful.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: My pleasure. Send me the revised survey before the weekend, and we'll look at it together.

sections.title: Talk on urban beekeeping
sections.context: A lecturer gives an informal talk to members of a local community group about the growth of beekeeping in cities, the rules involved and the practical challenges.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming. Today's talk is about urban beekeeping, which has grown quickly over the past decade. I'll cover three things: why cities have become attractive for bees, what you need to do before you start, and the practical problems that beekeepers face, especially in the summer months.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Let's start with a point that surprises many people. Cities can actually offer bees more flowers than the countryside does. Modern farmland is often covered by a single crop for much of the year, so bees have very little to feed on.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Parks, gardens and balconies, by contrast, usually contain a wide range of flowering plants, and those flowers keep blooming over a longer season. That is why most of the new hives in our city are in urban areas.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Where do you put the hive? This is one of the first questions beginners ask. Most of the hives in our city are placed on rooftops, because they are out of the way of people and pets. A rooftop also gives the bees a clear flight path.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: If you don't have a roof, a secure corner of a large garden can work, as long as the entrance faces away from the path.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, the legal side. Before you bring a single colony home, you must register it with the national bee register. The registration is free and takes about ten minutes online, but it is compulsory. The register helps the authorities track disease, and it also means that your neighbours can contact you quickly if a swarm escapes.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Many beginners forget this step, so please don't be one of them.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Let's talk about the bees themselves. A healthy colony in the middle of summer can contain up to sixty thousand bees, and that number can change very quickly. Most of the work is done by the workers, who are all female.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: They make the honey, look after the young and guard the entrance. The queen's only job is to lay eggs, so she's not really in charge of anything in the way people imagine.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Foraging is where the real journey happens. Individual bees can travel up to three kilometres from the hive in search of nectar and pollen. That's a long way for an insect that weighs less than a paperclip. In a city, this means that a hive on one side of the river can use gardens on the other side, which is one reason urban honey often has such a complex flavour.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The position of the hive also matters for the bees' health. Hives should face south-east, so they catch the morning sun. That warms the colony early, so the bees can leave the hive sooner, and it also helps to dry out the wet conditions that encourage mould.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Keep the hive away from strong winds, and make sure there is a shallow tray of water nearby, because bees need water to cool the hive in hot weather.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Inspection is the next topic. In the active season, you should check each hive every seven days. A thorough inspection takes time, but it's the only way to spot problems early, such as a queen who has stopped laying or a colony that is preparing to swarm.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Keep a notebook, because it's easy to forget what you saw two weeks ago, and the notes will also help you spot patterns.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, the biggest threat. Many beginners expect the weather or the lack of flowers to be the main danger, but in reality it is a parasite called varroa. This mite feeds on the bees and spreads viruses from one colony to another.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: If you don't treat it, the colony will usually die within a couple of years. The treatments are straightforward, but you must follow the timing carefully, and you must test regularly to see whether the mite count is rising.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Finally, the reward. A good hive in a productive year can produce around twenty kilograms of honey, although the amount varies enormously from one season to the next. Most urban beekeepers don't sell their honey, they share it with neighbours or give it away.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Some groups also run small projects with schools, which is a lovely way to introduce children to the natural world.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: If you'd like to learn more, we run beginners' workshops for new members. They take place at the community centre on Saturday mornings, and they include a hands-on session with a real hive. You don't need any experience, and you don't need to buy any equipment until you've decided that beekeeping is right for you.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Please sign up at the front desk after the talk, and bring a notebook. Thank you for listening, and I'll take questions now.
